newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Defiant Netanyahu says even U.S. can't budge him.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Netanyahu says even U.S. can't budge him.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing mounting Arab pressure to spur foundering peace talks, said on Sunday he will stand firm on his bedrock policies, even at the cost of ties with crucial ally Washington.

"Regardless of the fact that our relationship with the U.S. is of the first rank of Israel's strategic assets, it is not the supreme asset. The supreme asset is our security, those things that are sacred to us, like Jerusalem," Netanyahu said.

He said he viewed Israeli opposition to certain Palestinian goals, including the return of Arab refugees to ancestral homes within the present borders of the Jewish state, as also among his nation's "supreme assets".
"If a regime should arise in the U.S. and say, 'You must give in on all this in exchange for relations with the United States', I will not give in," Netanyahu told Israel Radio.

Soon after his upset victory over Shimon Peres in May, Netanyahu alarmed Arabs and jolted Washington by rejecting the formula of trading occupied land for peace, a U.S.-endorsed principle that had fueled five years of tough Middle East talks.
He also nullified the previous Labour government's curbs on Jewish settlement. Until Netanyahu came to power Washington had long denounced the settlements as a major obstacle to peace.
Alluding to Peres' centre-left policies, Netanyhau said: "One view holds that we should neutralise ourselves in the face of the U.S., and whatever the Americans say, we should do."

Netanyahu said he had made it clear in talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton that "our policy is not to create any limitation on existing Jewish settlement, and if we decide on new settlements, it will not come as a surprise."

Syrian Foreign Minister Farouk al-Shara, turning up Arab heat on the Netanyahu government, said on Sunday Arab states have agreed to make a link between relations with Israel and progress in talks between the Jewish state and its neighbours.

The U.S-educated Netanyahu, who spent much of his public life on diplomatic assignment in the United States, said he believed Israel's "very good relations" with Washington would be preserved, but said he would resist pressure if necessary.
Citing a precedent for resistance to White House arm-twisting, he described then-president Ronald Reagan's displeasure over Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon.
"This friendly administration, this friendly president imposed sanctions on us, such as suspending delivery of F-16 fighters.
"We didn't say, 'There's nothing we can do'...we acted to convince them, first of all, that their step was a mistake."
"We also activated our ties with various elements in the U.S. in order to stand up to the pressure," he said, in an apparent reference to the pro-Israel lobby in the United States.
Israel's military is dependent on Washington for supplying the bulk of its advanced weapons systems, paid for in part by an annual $1.8 billion in U.S. aid.
The Jewish state, the largest single recipient of U.S. foreign aid, also receives more than $1.2 billion dollars a year in economic assistance from Washington.
Netanyahu pledged to "do my best" to reach understandings with Clinton and the U.S. Congress, but was careful to add:
"I make our work with the United States fit our interests, and do not adapt our interests to fit our ties with the U.S."
Analysts have said the U.S. presidential campaign has lent Netanyahu greater latitude, as Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole vie for the votes of pro-Israel Jews in key states.
